featuredDrafts.title: Incentives for Access: Changes in Admissions and Care Delivery for Metastatic Cancer Patients in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities, After the Patient-Driven Payment Model
featuredDrafts.abstract: Cancer patients experience suboptimal care in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs). Medicare’s Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) incentivized SNFs to admit complex patients, potentially promoting admissions without appropriate changes in care delivery.  To evaluate changes in SNF admissions, rehabilitation therapy volume, and chemotherapy/radiation around admission or discharge, following PDPM and COVID-19.  Adjusted interrupted time series examining 1,125,782 hospital stays from metastatic cancer patients, using 100% Traditional Medicare claims (2018–2021).  PDPM was associated with increased SNF admissions (0.47 pp/month; 95% CI: [0.17, 0.76]) and an immediate reduction in therapy volume (−24.95 minutes per day, 95% CI: [−26.40, −23.48]). Chemotherapy use remained low, but increased by 21% at PDPM implementation, without subsequent slope change (RR: 1.21; 95% CI: [1.01, 1.46]); radiation was unchanged. COVID-19 reversed admission gains. SNF admissions for metastatic cancer patients increased without sustained changes in cancer-relevant care delivery, warranting investigation of health outcomes and outcome-driven policy.

featuredDrafts.title: Sagittal imbalance and incident long-term care needs in older adults: the locomotive syndrome and health outcomes in the Aizu Cohort Study (LOHAS)
featuredDrafts.abstract: Sagittal imbalance in older adults causes impairments in standing and gait, leading to mobility limitations (defined as “locomotive syndrome” in Japan), which are risk factors for future long-term care needs. This study aimed to investigate whether sagittal imbalance is a risk factor for long-term care needs in older adults. The primary outcome was incident long-term care need, defined as a new certification in the national insurance system during a 5-year follow-up. Sagittal vertical axis (SVA) was measured on a standing whole-spine lateral radiograph. Bodily pain (SF-12) and physical function (3-m timed up and go [TUG] test) were assessed. By SVA categories, incident care needs were observed in 9.1%, 12.7%, and 31.0% of participants in the SVA 95 mm groups, respectively. featuredDrafts.title: Social Engagement Programs of Area Agencies on Aging: Understanding Efforts to Reduce Social Isolation and Loneliness Among Older Adults
featuredDrafts.abstract: Social isolation and loneliness in later life are major public health concerns associated with increased morbidity and premature mortality. Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) constitute the primary local infrastructure for aging services in the US.  To describe social engagement program types and partnership structures among AAAs and to examine rural–non-rural differences.  We analyzed data from the 2025 National Survey of AAAs (n = 449). Descriptive statistics summarized program and partnership prevalence; item-level Pearson chi-square tests with Bonferroni adjustments compared rural and non-rural agencies.  Most AAAs offered multiple social engagement programs; volunteer engagement (66.0%), arts and creative activities (62.2%), visiting/calling programs (57.7%), and technology engagement (55.5%) were common. Non-rural AAAs were more likely to offer visiting/calling, technology-based activities, and memory cafes, while rural AAAs were more likely to partner with public health units. Rural–non-rural differences suggest context-specific influences of resources and infrastructure on program availability.

featuredDrafts.title: Structural Vulnerability and the Pandemic: Widening Gaps in Nursing Home Antipsychotic Prescribing
featuredDrafts.abstract: To assess whether national reductions in antipsychotic prescribing in U.S. nursing homes were shared equitably or masked widening gaps between top and bottom performers, we examined distributional trends across facilities from 2013 to 2023 using national facility-level data (CMS Provider Data Catalog; LTCFocus). We modeled long-stay antipsychotic measure performance using linear quantile mixed regression, assessed mobility across performance quartiles with transition matrices, and evaluated facility characteristics associated with trajectories. From 2013 to 2019, prescribing fell across all quantiles, with the steepest reductions among the worst performers, narrowing gaps with the best. After 2020, progress diverged: lower-performing facilities experienced sharp setbacks while top performers maintained gains. Mobility analyses showed entrenched disadvantage, with bottom-quartile facilities disproportionately likely to remain there. Higher Medicaid share predicted decline, whereas higher star ratings predicted improvement. The pandemic reversed earlier equity gains, amplifying structural disparities and exposing unequal capacity to sustain improvement.

featuredDrafts.title: Ambivalent return: Older adults’ homecoming after wartime displacement
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Little is known about how older adults experience their return home after wartime displacement, particularly when home and community are altered or remain insecure. This longitudinal qualitative study examined continuity and change across the displacement–return transition.  Twelve participants (aged 65–92), previously interviewed during displacement (T1), were re-interviewed after returning home (T2) using a qualitative descriptive approach with thematic analysis.  Three themes emerged: (1) the unsettled return, involving altered security, unfamiliarity within the home, and disrupted community life; (2) continuity of social relationships and activities after return; and (3) shifts in life perspective and self-perception. These themes describe the shared dimensions of post-return experience, whereas the complementary diachronic analysis examined how these dimensions changed and combined across T1 and T2. A diachronic analysis identified four return trajectories: functioning but incomplete; ambivalent or gradual return requiring active reorganization; return supported by communal and social continuity and use of personal resources; and ongoing erosion and unresolved damage. Discussion These findings demonstrate that return is not restoration but a reconfiguration of person-environment fit, place identity, belonging, and security in later life. For older adults, this transition involved rebuilding environmental familiarity, security, belonging, and agency rather than simply resuming pre-displacement life. The study highlights social infrastructure as critical for post-return adaptation, underscoring the need for policies recognizing the return process as a significant transition requiring continued communal support.

featuredDrafts.title: Transportation Use, Trip Taking, and Trip Purposes Among Older Adults Not in the Labor Force: Evidence From the 2022 National Household Travel Survey
featuredDrafts.abstract: Transportation needs may differ by labor-force participation status, yet little is known about travel behavior among older adults not in the labor force.  To examine alternative transportation use, trip taking, and trip purposes among older adults not in the labor force.  Data came from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey ( N = 3,474; aged ≥65; not in the labor force). Logistic regression models examined factors associated with transportation mode, taking any trip on the assigned reporting day, and trip purposes.  Nearly 87% drove, 5%–7% used rideshare/taxi, public transit, or bicycles, and one-third walked for transportation. Transportation use and trip-taking varied by socioeconomic characteristics, living arrangements, and digital engagement. Drivers, transportation walkers, and college graduates were more likely to travel. Social/recreational trips were more common among those living alone and among college graduates.  Improving transportation accessibility, affordability, and digital literacy may support late-life mobility and community participation.

featuredDrafts.title: Reducing Stress in Caregivers of People With Dementia in Psychiatric Care: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of an Emotion-Focused Group Intervention
featuredDrafts.abstract: Caregivers of people with dementia (CPwD) are at higher risk for psychological stress and mental health issues.  This study evaluated the effectiveness of a brief, four-session group intervention combining socio-medical education, mindfulness and emotion-focused support in reducing stress and improving psychological outcomes in an acute psychiatric hospital setting.  A within-subject waiting-period control design with repeated measures was conducted with N = 52 CPwD. Assessments were performed at baseline, pre-intervention, post-intervention and follow-up. Changes across phases were analyzed using subsequent contrast analyses.  Following the intervention, perceived stress decreased significantly ( p = .038) and general functioning improved ( p = .002) at follow-up. No significant changes were found for depressive symptoms or subjective well-being. The study protocol was designed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the joint Ethics Committee of the medical faculty at the Ludwig-Maximilians-University of Munich (project number 22-0995).

featuredDrafts.title: Rethinking Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Severe Alzheimer's Disease: From Intentional Explanation to an Ecological, Body–Environment Framework
featuredDrafts.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
featuredDrafts.abstract: In contemporary dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are often understood as expressions of the person's intentions or needs. This paper examines the limits of understanding BPSD as “expressions of intention” in severe Alzheimer's disease. It argues that while desires may still be preserved, the formation and maintenance of beliefs—an essential constituent of intentions in the standard desire–belief model—are likely to be severely compromised. As a result, many behavioral and perceptual symptoms closely related to basic activities of daily living cannot be adequately explained within an intention-based framework. As a complementary framework to existing dementia care theories, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of BPSD as arising from the interaction between embodied procedural memory and environmental affordances. Many BPSD are better understood not as expressions of intention, but as the outcome of situational and non-selective reactivation of fragments of relatively preserved procedural memory in response to the structure of the immediate environment. This reconceptualization extends the focus of care practice beyond the interpretation of the presumed meanings or intentions underlying BPSD and highlights the importance of modifying care environments in ways that appropriately support or constrain the reactivation of procedural memory.

featuredDrafts.title: Understandings of Ageism and Healthcare in the COVID-19 Pandemic
featuredDrafts.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
featuredDrafts.abstract: Ageism is widespread and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, with resource shortages contributing to healthcare guidelines that systematically deprioritised older adults. Whilst the ethical considerations of these guidelines are well documented, perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare allocation remain underexplored. This study examined younger and older adults’ perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare during COVID-19 through a social identity approach. Using a story completion method, 22 older and 41 younger adult participants completed a story about a younger or older COVID-19 patient and doctors allocating the last available ventilator. Using thematic analysis, three themes were developed: (1) age determines health, (2) age determines the value of life, and (3) age determines acceptance of death.  support the need for policies protecting against the influence of ageism in healthcare systems and emphasise the need to understand how internalised ageism may influence perceptions and health behaviours of older patients.

featuredDrafts.title: ‘Keeping me sharp”: Self-perceived effects of grandparenthood on cognition: An exploratory thematic analysis
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: The experience of grandparenthood holds the potential for novel and engaging social interactions and activities, which may protect against cognitive decline. The present study outlines how individuals believe grandparenthood has impacted their cognitive abilities in late life.  We asked 127 grandparents (87 grandmothers and 40 grandfathers) how they thought grandparenthood had impacted their mental ability (memory, concentration, and cognitive ability). An exploratory thematic analysis utilizing a codebook approach was conducted on the participant responses.  Analysis revealed four major themes among the responses: “grandparenthood as a continuous experience that promotes healthy cognitive functioning”, “shifting perspectives”, “limited interaction”, and “the negative impacts of grandparenthood.” Discussion A majority of grandparents expressed the belief that interacting with their grandchildren is beneficial to their cognition. However, some participants qualified grandparenthood as a stressful experience that has negatively impacted their cognitive health. These findings support previous literature showing both cognitive benefits associated with grandparental caregiving and negative cognitive outcomes that may result from the stress of caregiving.

featuredDrafts.title: Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) and Cognition: A Scoping Review
featuredDrafts.abstract: To map the evidence of disparities in cognition across different social determinants of health (SDOH), examine how SDOH are measured in the context of research on cognitive outcomes and identify knowledge gaps. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched. We included peer-reviewed studies of adults that examined SDOH as primary exposures in relation to cognitive outcomes, and described a SDOH framework or definition in the context of cognition. Non-human studies, case reports, case series, editorials, protocols, and -only records were excluded. Ninety-one records were included. Most of the included studies were conducted in the US and the most frequently used framework was the Healthy People (2030) framework. Among studies examining a single SDOH indicator, the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) was the most used measure. Most of the existing research failed to explain the concept of SDOH and lacked a framework to guide the inclusion and interpretation of SDOH indicators. SDOH measures were heterogeneous across studies, with many examining only a single indicator and limited use of multidimensional approaches. This heterogeneity made findings challenging to compare. More research is needed on multidimensional SDOH and cognition in various racial/ethnic groups and less-studied geographic and cultural contexts, under explicit SDOH frameworks.

featuredDrafts.title: Control Beliefs and Emotional Aspects of Psychological Frailty Among Couples in Later Life
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study investigated the associations between control beliefs and the emotional aspects of psychological frailty (i.e., depression, anxiety, and loneliness) among older married couples.  Multivariate Actor-Partner Interdependence Models were used to analyze data from 538 couples aged 65 or older, drawn from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study.  Individuals’ own control beliefs were consistently associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, and loneliness for both spouses. A partner effect emerged for loneliness, with wives’ control beliefs associated with lower levels of loneliness in their husbands, but this was not significant after adjusting for marital support and strain. Discussion These findings identify control beliefs as a consistent individual-level protective factor. Interventions to improve emotional well-being in older couples should prioritize strengthening personal control beliefs. Dyadic processes merit further investigation, particularly for outcomes such as loneliness that are closely embedded in the relational context.

featuredDrafts.title: Latent Structures of Social Determinants of Health in Later Life: A Comparison of U.S.-Born and Immigrants
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study examined whether the latent structure of social determinants of health (SDOH) differs by nativity and how they relate to health outcomes in later life.  Using 2016–2018 HRS data, exploratory factor analyses by nativity were conducted, followed by nativity-stratified regressions linking SDOH factors to health outcomes.  Four comparable factors emerged in both groups: neighborhood environment, interpersonal stressors, socioeconomic resources, and family support. Loading patterns showed modest nativity differences: among immigrants, social isolation aligned more strongly with family support than socioeconomic resources and perceived discrimination loaded weakly on interpersonal stressors. Interpersonal stressors were associated with poorer mental and cognitive health in both groups; socioeconomic resources were associated with better health outcomes but more weakly among immigrants. Associations of neighborhood environment and family support with health varied by nativity. Discussion Findings indicate substantial commonality in SDOH structures alongside suggestive nativity-related differences, warranting replication in larger immigrant samples.

featuredDrafts.title: Does the Pilot Long-Term Care Insurance Work as Expected in China? Examining its Impact on Hospital Utilizations, Medical Expenses, and Health
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study investigates the impact of long-term care insurance (LTCI) on older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Using national representative data from four waves of CHARLS (2011, 2013, 2015, 2018), we find that LTCI decreases older adults’ monthly outpatient visits but is associated with an increase in both annual inpatient stays and inpatient medical expenses. Further evidence suggests that older adults covered by the pilot LTCI program have better health status compared to their counterparts in non-pilot cities. Overall, findings offer empirical support for the role of the LTCI program in Chinese older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Findings of China’s LTCI may offer insights for other countries with a large aging population but with no feasible LTCI framework.

featuredDrafts.title: Association Between a Hybrid Video-Guided Multicomponent Exercise Program With Staff Assistance and Free-Living Gait in Older Adults With Knee and Low Back Pain: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
featuredDrafts.abstract: Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as  indicators of mobility.  In this study, we aimed to examine the effects of a 12-week hybrid exercise-based program on daily-life walking characteristics.  A total of 59 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥65 years) with mild to moderate knee and/or low back pain were randomized to either a hybrid exercise group or an educational control group. Daily-life walking was monitored using an ankle sensor. Daily observation data were collected within 2 planned 7-day windows. Primary parameters included activity volume and gait characteristics. Statistical analyses were conducted based on a modified intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models, with a per-protocol set used for sensitivity analyses.  The mixed-effects analysis based on the modified intention-to-treat principle (n=52 participants; 696 observations) suggested an effect of the intervention on improving walking quality, particularly step length (β=2.39 cm; P =.04; Hedges g =0.493), with a smaller effect with borderline statistical significance observed on improving walking speed (β=0.05 m/s; P =.06; Hedges g =0.496). Cadence, daily distance, daily steps, active energy expenditure, and accumulated 3 or more metabolic equivalent of task activities showed no clear difference between the groups. In the per-protocol sensitivity analysis (n=44), the same directional pattern of improvement was observed for step length (β=1.95 cm; P =.13; Hedges g =0.365) and walking speed (β=0.04 m/s; P =.14; Hedges g =0.368); however, the estimates were imprecise.  A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.

featuredDrafts.title: Socioeconomic Differences in the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Episodic Memory Trajectories in Midlife and Old Age
featuredDrafts.abstract: : Episodic memory trajectories vary substantially between individuals in the second half of life: some maintain high levels of performance into their 80s, whereas others experience marked declines as early as their 50s. Identifying factors that help explain this heterogeneity is critical for understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on the resource substitution hypothesis and the Openness–Fluid–Crystallized–Intelligence (OFCI) model, this preregistered study examined whether the Big Five personality traits and their interactions with socioeconomic status (SES) predict individual differences in episodic memory trajectories, testing also potential non-linear associations. We expected higher openness and lower neuroticism to be associated with better memory levels and slower decline, with stronger effects at lower levels of SES. : We analyzed data from 57,947 individuals aged 50 and older (M = 67.78, SD = 9.03) who participated in at least two waves (7, 8, or 9) of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Multilevel growth models were used to estimate associations between personality and episodic memory levels and 5-year change, and whether SES (i.e., education, income, and wealth) moderated these associations. : Consistent with the OFCI model and the resource substitution hypothesis, higher openness was associated with better episodic memory levels, particularly among individuals with lower wealth. Higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness were linked to poorer episodic memory levels, but only among less wealthy individuals. Higher extraversion was associated with better memory levels overall, and individuals at the extremes of extraversion exhibited somewhat flatter declines compared to those with moderate levels. Except for extraversion, there was little evidence for non-linear associations or for associations with 5-year change in episodic memory. : Our findings underscore the relevance of wealth as an important socioeconomic resource for cognitive health beyond income and education, particularly in old age, when income is typically reduced. Overall, the  support modest concurrent associations between personality, SES, and episodic memory levels, but provide hardly any evidence for longitudinal effects. More frequent and longer-term longitudinal assessments are needed to clarify potential effects on cognitive aging.

featuredDrafts.title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study
featuredDrafts.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of  impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.  This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.  We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.  Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and F 1 -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns.  A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.

featuredDrafts.title: Blind giving predicts longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility in later life
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Financial fraud is a common and consequential threat among older adults, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 4% to 17% annually. Although cognitive decline has been widely studied as a risk factor, less is known about behavioral characteristics that may predict changes in scam susceptibility. In the present study, we examined whether blind giving predicted trajectories of scam susceptibility across a two-year period and whether this association differed as a function of age. Research Design and  One hundred and sixteen cognitively unimpaired older adults (aged 51 to 83; 72% female) completed a behavioral economic measure of blind giving at baseline and a self-report measure of scam susceptibility annually across three visits.  Linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant interaction between time, blind giving, and age (p = .022), such that greater baseline blind giving was associated with increasing scam susceptibility over time among relatively older participants, whereas scam susceptibility remained stable across levels of blind giving among relatively younger participants. Blind giving was not associated with scam susceptibility at baseline (p = .515), and the longitudinal association persisted after separately adjusting for global cognition, socioeconomic status, and race (all ps ≤ .026).  Greater blind giving predicted longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility over a two-year period, with this pattern observed specifically in advanced age. These findings suggest that prosocial tendencies may become maladaptive in later life, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk individuals to inform prevention efforts in aging populations.

featuredDrafts.title: Heat stress and coping strategies among older adults in three Sunbelt cities in the United States
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Prevailing scientific evidence suggests that extreme heat poses a substantial threat to the health and well-being of older adults in the Sunbelt cities of the United States. However, prior research has not adequately addressed the specific socio-demographic, health-related vulnerabilities, and coping-strategic factors influencing heat stress among older urban populations.  Informed by the Socio-Ecological Model, this study adopts a retrospective cohort study design to investigate the predictors and experiences of heat stress among older adults. Data from older adults in Los Angeles, Houston, and Phoenix were analyzed using thematic and multiple binary logistic regression analyses.  The  reveal that much older adults (aged 80 +) were less likely to experience heat stress compared to their relatively younger counterparts. Also, marital status, income, respiratory diseases, physical activity, taking cool showers, and city of residence were significantly associated with a higher risk of suffering heat stress. The qualitative  uncovered individual-level behavioural adjustment as an effective coping mechanism during extreme heat events.  These  underscore the complex interplay of behavioral, socio-demographic, and health-related factors influencing heat stress among older adults. The study recommends that urban health strategies prioritize these demographics, enhancing support systems and coping mechanisms to reduce vulnerability to heat stress among older urban populations.

featuredDrafts.title: Being Sensed, Scored, and ‘Connected’: A Social-Gerontological Critique of AI-Driven Loneliness Detection for Older Adults in Taiwan
featuredDrafts.abstract: Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) that continuously infers emotion promises to change how care systems identify older adults at risk of loneliness. We use AI-driven loneliness detection to mean systems that infer loneliness, or a proxy for it, from sensed data rather than from a person’s answer, rendering the inference as a score or category used in care; they range from facial and vocal emotion recognition to behavioral risk prediction from everyday activity data. Engineering feasibility, more than any social-gerontological understanding of loneliness, has driven this agenda, and little attention has gone to how older adults in different cultural contexts wish to be known and supported. Because such detection is not yet in routine use in Taiwan, this Forum article adopts an anticipatory-governance stance, examining before deployment a trajectory that policy makes plausible. Anchored in Taiwan’s ageing society and long-term care system, it argues that culturally responsive design should begin with older adults’ own meanings, relational obligations, and expectations of privacy and autonomy, not with the sensors. It identifies three tensions for social gerontology: the reframing of a relational experience as an individual biometric deficit; the risk that algorithms read culturally patterned emotional restraint as noise; and the slippage from care toward surveillance once risk indices enter routine care workflows. Taking seriously the case for technological augmentation of scarce care resources, the article proposes principles for a socially accountable approach and a research agenda on how older adults negotiate being sensed, scored, and ‘connected.’

featuredDrafts.title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort
featuredDrafts.abstract: Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.  This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.  This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.  At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.  Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

archiveRecords.title: Development of an exploratory preoperative laboratory-based score for 24-month mortality after major lower extremity amputation in geriatric diabetic foot patients
archiveRecords.abstract: Major lower extremity amputation for diabetic foot complications is associated with substantial mortality, particularly in older adults. We evaluated whether routinely available preoperative laboratory parameters provide prognostic information for 24-month mortality and developed an exploratory laboratory-based risk score.  This retrospective cohort study included 72 patients aged ≥ 65 years who underwent transtibial or transfemoral amputation for diabetic foot complications between January 2021 and June 2023 at a tertiary referral center. Vital status was ascertained through July 31, 2025. Associations with 24-month all-cause mortality were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression. A 3-point score was derived from laboratory predictors using receiver operating characteristic analysis and Youden-index-based thresholds. Model discrimination and calibration were assessed, and bootstrap optimism correction was applied to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. The proposed score was additionally compared with the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI), and Hemoglobin–Albumin–Lymphocyte–Platelet (HALP) score.  Thirty-nine patients (54.2%) died within 24 months. Kaplan–Meier-estimated 24-month survival was 45.8% (95% CI 34.1–56.8%). In multivariable Cox analysis, higher hemoglobin (adjusted HR 1.302, 95% CI 1.041–1.628; p = 0.021), lower platelet count (adjusted HR 0.9966, 95% CI 0.9939–0.9994; p = 0.017), and lower albumin (adjusted HR 0.868, 95% CI 0.813–0.927; p 10.3 g/dL, platelet count p  A simple score based on albumin, hemoglobin, and platelet count showed promising prognostic discrimination for 24-month mortality after major amputation in this geriatric diabetic foot cohort. Quantitative ischemia severity and standardized neuropathy and frailty assessments were unavailable, and the score was derived and evaluated in the same derivation cohort, while bootstrap optimism correction was limited to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. It should therefore be regarded as exploratory, should not replace comprehensive clinical and vascular assessment, and requires external validation before clinical use.

archiveRecords.title: Impact of malnutrition and protein-enriched oral nutrition on early recovery after fragility fractures in older adults: the NuTra trial
archiveRecords.abstract: Malnutrition is highly prevalent in geriatric trauma patients and is associated with impaired recovery, complications, and reduced likelihood of returning home. Nonetheless, the impact of a targeted protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay on patient outcome and rehabilitation remains to be investigated. Materials and  This single-center randomized controlled study enrolled patients ≥ 70 years with fragility fractures admitted to a Level I trauma center. Nutritional status was assessed using the Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 and Mini Nutritional Assessment. Patients screened positive in ≥ 1 tool were classified as being at nutritional risk and randomized to a protein-enriched diet (Group A) or standard diet (Group B); patients with negative screening served as observational reference group without nutritional risk (Group C). The intervention targeted 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protein. Primary outcomes were in-hospital medical complications, surgical site infections and functional mobility at discharge. Secondary outcomes included length of stay, discharge destination, and in-hospital mortality. Multinomial logistic regression assessed independent associations with discharge destination.  Of the 218 patients (mean age 81.8 ± 6.9 years; 72.0% female), 100 (45.9%) screened positive for being at nutritional risk and were randomized to intervention (A, n = 46) or control (B, n = 54), while 118 (54.1%) patients without nutritional risk served as reference group (C). Patients at nutritional risk showed higher comorbidity burdens, higher ASA classes, and greater frailty than group C. Medical complications occurred in 45.0% of patients, with no significant differences between groups. Serum albumin decreased and CRP increased during hospitalization, without differences among the groups. Patients in reference group C were more often independently mobile and discharged home, whereas all patients at nutritional risk more frequently required institutional care. In multivariable analysis, a higher age-adjusted CCI was independently associated with discharge destination, whereas no independent effect of the nutritional intervention was observed.  In this geriatric trauma cohort, being at nutritional risk was closely linked to frailty and multimorbidity. A protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay did not translate into measurable short-term benefits regarding complications, functional mobility, length of stay or discharge destination. Nutritional risk should therefore be considered within the broader context of overall vulnerability, and nutritional care may need to be embedded in comprehensive longitudinal rehabilitation strategies extending beyond the acute in-hospital phase. Trial registration The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on 12 May 2026 (NCT07582575).

archiveRecords.title: Activity diversity and psychological richness across midlife and older adulthood
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Psychological richness, a dimension of well-being characterized by novelty, complexity, and perspective change, is theoretically grounded in varied and unusual experiences. This study examined whether daily activity diversity was associated with psychological richness in two cohorts of midlife and older adults from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study.  Daily reports were drawn from two cohorts of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study: MIDUS 2 (M2; N = 1,834) and the MIDUS Refresher (MR; N = 730). Daily activity diversity was quantified with Shannon entropy, capturing both the breadth and evenness of participants' daily activities.  Lower activity diversity was associated with higher psychological richness in both cohorts (M2: β = −0.07, p Discussion These findings suggest that broader activity repertoires do not necessarily correspond to greater psychological richness and that psychologically rich lives may coexist with relatively narrow patterns of daily engagement.

archiveRecords.title: Crossing the Digital Divide: Understanding Older Adults’ Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Qualitative Study
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence is redefining the relationship between older adults and digital technologies. Existing studies have largely explained the digital divide among older adults through traditional digital media such as smartphones and mobile payment, while insufficient attention has been paid to how conversational artificial intelligence changes older adults’ entry thresholds, sustained-use motivations, and risk-judgment mechanisms. This study adopts a multimethod qualitative design, with semistructured interviews as the primary method and digital scenario-based tasks as a complementary method. From January to February 2026, the study was conducted in Chedun Town and Xinqiao Town, Songjiang District, Shanghai, with 40 participants aged 60 and above who had internet-use experience and showed a pronounced tendency toward high-frequency smartphone use. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Interview transcripts, task-observation records, screenshots of AI conversations, and field notes were triangulated; an initial coding manual, double review, and consensus discussion were used to enhance analytic credibility. The study finds that generative artificial intelligence shifts the technological threshold from procedural operation to need articulation and result evaluation, enabling some older adults to compensate for limitations in traditional interface operation through life experience and language-expression skills. Older adults’ sustained use is not driven simply by efficiency, but is closely related to emotional anchoring in later life, experience organization, relationship maintenance, and concrete task handling. Community support, peer learning, and intergenerational assistance constitute important mediating mechanisms through which older adults move from initial experimentation to stable use. Whether older adults truly cross the digital divide depends on whether they can develop the capacities of source verification, contextual delimitation, and boundary judgment. Based on these findings, the study proposes a “conditional crossing” mechanism for older adults’ acceptance of AI technologies and argues that age-friendly governance should move beyond interface simplification toward capability enhancement and risk support.

archiveRecords.title: Age-associated differences in lower-extremity muscle mass, force, and power in older adults: a cross-sectional analysis of sex differences
archiveRecords.abstract: The decline in musculoskeletal function with aging is a key contributor to mobility impairments and loss of independence. While sarcopenia and dynapenia are well described, recent evidence highlights muscle power as a more sensitive indicator of functional deterioration. Aims This study aimed to compare age-associated differences in muscle mass, force, and lower-limb muscle power in older adults over different assessment , while accounting for sex-related differences.  Three hundred nineteen community-dwelling adults aged 60–97 years were assessed for muscle mass (DXA-derived lean mass, appendicular skeletal muscle mass index), muscle force (handgrip force, knee extension maximal isometric contraction), muscle moments and angular velocity (isokinetic dynamometry), and lower-limb muscle power (isokinetic testing and sit-to-stand power). Associations with age and sex were examined using regression models and ANOVA.  Lower-limb muscle power showed a stronger negative association with age than muscle force or mass (β = − 0.433 vs. − 0.303 and − 0.119, respectively; p  Lower-limb muscle power appeared more sensitive to age-associated differences than muscle force or mass, supporting its role as a key biomarker of neuromuscular aging. This study also highlights that sex may contribute to variability in age-associated patterns of muscle power, raising questions about the universality of its definition that warrant further confirmation. These findings emphasize the clinical importance of including power assessments in strategies to preserve independence in older adults. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05343286, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05343286 .

archiveRecords.title: Diagnostic performance of calculated serum osmolarity versus clinical impression for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients
archiveRecords.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and agreement of calculated serum osmolarity for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients, using clinical impression of dehydration as the reference standard, and to examine glucose levels across concordant and discordant classification groups. Design and setting This prospective, observational study was conducted in a geriatric acute care unit. Participants The study included 455 older hospitalized patients with a mean age of 82.2 ± 6.8 years and 70% were female. Measurements Clinical impression of dehydration (dehydration vs. no dehydration [normal hydration + hyperhydration]) was judged and recorded by the attending physician within 24 h of admission. Calculated serum osmolarity was derived from routine laboratory values and classified as high (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) or normal (  Clinically, 23% of patients were classified as dehydrated. High calculated osmolarity occurred in 38%. Using the ≥ 295 mOsmol/l cut-off, sensitivity was 48.6% and specificity 65.1%; positive and negative predictive values were 29.7% and 80.7%, respectively, and accuracy was 61.3%. Agreement beyond chance was poor (κ = 0.112). Mean glucose was higher in osmolarity-positive groups, including false positives (all p  In older hospitalized patients, calculated serum osmolarity (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) showed limited agreement with clinical dehydration assessment with frequent osmolarity-positive classifications in clinically non-dehydrated patients. These findings support cautious clinical interpretation of calculated osmolarity in acute care, particularly when glucose is elevated.

archiveRecords.title: Body weight following a multidomain lifestyle intervention in older adults at risk of dementia – A post-hoc analysis of the AgeWell.de-trial
archiveRecords.abstract: Lifestyle interventions provide a promising approach to address higher body weight as a risk factor for dementia.  The AgeWell.de-trial was primarily designed to preserve cognitive function and reduce dementia risk. In this post-hoc analysis, we investigated body weight following the multidomain intervention among older adults with overweight or obesity, as well as the role of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss.  Analyses used data from the cluster-randomized AgeWell.de-trial, testing a multidomain intervention (dietary counselling, enhancement of physical, social and cognitive activity, medication review, intervention for cardiovascular risk factors, depressive symptoms/grief, if applicable) over 24 months in adults aged 60 to 77 years at risk for dementia. Associations between intervention allocation and body weight at follow-up were analyzed using linear regression, controlling for covariates, based on multiply imputed data.  The sample included n = 678 participants with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², mean age (SD): 68.9 (4.8), 52.1% female. Group allocation was not associated with body weight at 24-month follow-up (b (unstandardized regression coefficient) = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.51; 1.11). Older age (b = -0.14, 95% CI: -0.25; -0.03) and a high level of education (b = -1.28, 95% CI: -2.55; 0.00) were linked to lower body weight at follow-up, while higher baseline body weight predicted higher body weight at follow-up (b = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.91; 0.98). Levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss remained high but stable in both groups, regardless of group allocation.  In this post-hoc analysis, group allocation was not associated with lower body weight at follow-up. Despite high levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss and favorable changes in diet and physical activity in the intervention group, these changes did not translate into measurable weight loss. Trial registration AgeWell.de was prospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register on December 7th, 2017 (DRKS trial identifier DRKS00013555).

archiveRecords.title: Two-assessment patterns of past-year hospitalization reporting and subsequent functional deterioration and mortality among older adults in China: a two-window longitudinal prognostic factor study
archiveRecords.abstract: Past-year hospitalization reports may identify older adults with adverse subsequent prognosis, but two assessments do not continuously observe hospital use and their incremental information beyond one-wave reporting is uncertain.  We analysed two three-wave windows of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS): 2011 (Wave 1) and 2013 (Wave 2) hospitalization reports with 2015 (Wave 3) outcomes, and 2013 (Wave 2) and 2015 (Wave 3) reports with 2018 (Wave 4) outcomes. Patterns were 00 (neither assessment), 01 (second only), 10 (first only) and 11 (both). The prespecified primary analysis compared 11 with 00 for survivor-conditional ADL deterioration (increase ≥1) among participants with observed outcome-assessment ADL. Modified Poisson models used community-clustered robust covariance and 50 multiply imputed datasets. Four-pattern, one-wave, mortality, composite, sequential complete-covariate, cognition missing-not-at-random (MNAR), and inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting (IPCW) analyses were also examined.  ADL deterioration occurred in 932/4,365 observed survivors in Window 1 and 961/4,911 in Window 2. Adjusted RRs for 11 versus 00 were 1.230 (95% CI 1.007–1.502) and 1.094 (0.906–1.320), respectively. RRs for 11 versus pooled 01 + 10 were 1.229 (1.000–1.511) and 1.019 (0.845–1.228). Mortality RRs were 1.461 (0.986–2.166) and 1.482 (1.187–1.849), and death-or-deterioration RRs were 1.240 (1.054–1.459) and 1.166 (1.031–1.319). In fixed complete-covariate sequential analyses, 11-versus-00 point estimates moved markedly toward or below the null after multidimensional health adjustment, with wide confidence intervals. Cognition MNAR estimates changed little; IPCW point estimates were similar in magnitude (Window 1 RR 1.222, 95% CI 0.999–1.494; Window 2 RR 1.092, 0.905–1.317).  The 11 pattern marked less favorable prognosis relative to 00, but the survivor-conditional functional association varied across calendar windows and analytic strategies, and two reports did not consistently distinguish risk from one-wave reporting. These related within-cohort windows do not constitute independent replication.  support cautious prognostic interpretation, not a causal effect, verified recurrent-admission measure or stand-alone screening rule.

archiveRecords.title: Enhanced person profiles: a cluster randomised trial protocol for Swiss long-term care facilities
archiveRecords.abstract: Family participation and teamwork are crucial components of person-centred dementia care in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) and are therefore widely recommended. However, these often remain ad hoc and staff-dependent in LTCF settings. Robust evidence on reproducible whole-team models for family participation and their impact on the quality of life of people with dementia is limited. The person profile is a complex intervention that has been tested under randomised controlled trial conditions, but family participation and teamwork were identified as weak areas in this intervention. Consequently, we developed the enhanced person profile. This programme incorporates clinical tools for routine family participation and psychological safety  that enhance teamwork, ultimately aiming to improve the quality of life of people with dementia.  We will conduct a two-period, two-sequence cluster randomised crossover trial in 20 LTCFs in German-speaking Switzerland with 260 people with dementia. Each period will last 7 months, separated by a 1-month washout. Clusters will follow one of two sequences (intervention → usual care or usual care → intervention). The primary outcome will be proxy-rated quality of life (QUALIDEM). Secondary outcomes will comprise symptoms and concerns (Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale for People with Dementia (IPOS-Dem)), person-centred care (Person-Centred Practice Inventory – Staff Short Form (PCPI-S SF)), perceived family participation (FICS-T), and teamwork (Team Climate Inventory (TCI); unit). Our analyses will be carried out using linear mixed-effects models under the intention-to-treat principle, accounting for clustering and repeated measures. A mixed- process evaluation will be employed to examine implementation, mechanisms, and context, with qualitative follow-up exploring sustainability. Discussion This trial, embedded in routine LTCF care, will assess the effects of the enhanced person profile on the quality of life of people with dementia and determine its mechanisms of action as well as implementation requirements for large-scale adoption. Trial registration This trial was registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00041653). The Berne Cantonal Ethics Committee (lead committee) reviewed and approved the protocol and study documents, including the consent forms, educational materials, and electronic case report forms (BASEC-ID: 2026 − 00761).

archiveRecords.title: Physical, psychological, and cognitive multimorbidity patterns and the risk of disability among older adults in China: a prospective cohort study
archiveRecords.abstract: Physical disorders frequently co-occur with psychological and cognitive conditions, increasing the risk of disability. However, the specific disability risks associated with distinct multimorbidity patterns remain unclear. This study aimed to examine the differential risks of disability associated with various combinations of physical, psychological, and cognitive disorders.  Data were obtained from the 2018 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, involving 5186 adults aged 60 and older with a 2-year follow-up. Modified Poisson regression models were utilized to assess associations between multimorbidity patterns and disability risk, stratified by age and sex. Relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.  Five disease patterns were identified: only physical disorders, psychological or cognitive disorders, physical-cognitive multimorbidity, physical-psychological multimorbidity, and physical-psychological-cognitive multimorbidity. Compared to participants without disorders, four patterns were significantly associated with disability after two years. Specifically, physical-psychological-cognitive multimorbidity presented the highest risk (aRR = 4.02, 95%CI:2.94–5.50), followed by physical-psychological multimorbidity (aRR = 3.30, 95%CI:2.40–4.54), physical-cognitive multimorbidity (aRR = 2.20, 95%CI:1.60–3.03), and only physical disorders (aRR = 1.85, 95%CI:1.36–2.52). Subgroup analyses by age and sex yielded consistent .  This study demonstrates a graded increase in disability risk among older adults in China across various combinations of physical, psychological, and cognitive disorders, particularly when psychological conditions coexist with physical illnesses. These findings suggest that emotional and cognitive screenings should be integrated into routine geriatric assessments.

archiveRecords.title: Local RAGE Inhibition Attenuates Early Diabetic Retinal Pathology in Streptozotocin-Induced Rats
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Diabetic retinopathy, which occurs during extended periods of chronic hyperglycemia, is one of the main causes of vision loss. The receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) plays a central role in inflammatory and angiogenic signaling, both of which contribute to the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, but its therapeutic targeting in ocular disease has been insufficiently explored.  We evaluated topical RAGE229, a small-molecule RAGE inhibitor, and an intravitreally administered anti-RAGE antibody in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model. At day 84, treatment effects were assessed using masked fundoscopic scoring, RT-qPCR, immunohistochemistry, and histological morphometry. Treated eyes were evaluated against both route-matched diabetic vehicle-control groups and paired contralateral vehicle-treated eyes.  Both interventions reduced fundoscopic pathology and retinal Vegfa and Nfkb1 expression, whereas Ager showed only a non-significant downward trend. NF-κB p65 immunoreactivity was reduced by both treatments, while a significant reduction in VEGF-A immunoreactivity was detected only in the paired anti-RAGE antibody analysis. Morphometric analysis indicated attenuation of diabetes-associated retinal thinning with both interventions. Neither intervention altered systemic glycemic control. Although both interventions demonstrated similar overall anatomical protection, anti-RAGE antibody treatment showed more consistent effects across protein-level and structural endpoints.  These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that local RAGE-targeted treatment may attenuate vascular, molecular, and structural manifestations of early experimental diabetic retinopathy without detectable changes in systemic glycemia. Further preclinical studies should evaluate ocular exposure, direct target engagement, functional visual outcomes, and reproducibility in larger cohorts.

archiveRecords.title: Gaps Between Self-Reported and Documented Use of a Health Care Service Portal Among Older Adults: Cross-Sectional Survey and Retrospective Electronic Data Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Health care systems increasingly offer services to citizens through online portals, which have been found to be associated with patient satisfaction and better management of health concerns. Few studies have compared self-reported use with objectively documented portal use, especially among older adults.  This study aimed to examine differences between documented and self-reported health portal use, and their associations with  variables and digital health literacy (DHL) among older adults.  A cross-sectional telephone survey was conducted among 600 participants aged 60 years and older, who were sampled from a registry of members of a national health maintenance organization (HMO). The participants reported their use of the HMO’s portal, their DHL, and demographic and  variables. Participants’ use of the portal was retrospectively retrieved from the HMO’s administrative database.  A large gap between self-reported use and documented use of the health portal was found: for example, while only 8.1% (46/566) reported not using the portal, the HMO’s records indicated that 62% (372/600) did not make use of the portal. However, a positive correlation was found between self-reported use and documented use ( r =0.22; P r =0.41; P r =0.56; P P =.02) and ethnicity (β=−0.22; P r =0.09; P= .04), was not significantly associated with documented use in this analysis (β=0.02; P =.97).  The findings indicate that users tend to overestimate their health portal use. Interpretations vary from measurement issues, such as social desirability bias regarding digital functioning or the perception that assisted use also constitutes usage, to signaling their identity as engaged digital health consumers. Future studies on digital health use should also include measures of electronically documented use and not only self-reported use.

archiveRecords.title: Multi-Domain Intrinsic Capacity Decline and Fall History Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Rural Taiwan: Implications for ICOPE-Based Community Screening
archiveRecords.abstract: While WHO ICOPE screening is routine, the association between multi-domain intrinsic capacity (IC) decline and falls remains understudied in community-based gerontology practice.  This study analysed 775 rural older adults (mean age 79.4) with ≥1 IC abnormality using multivariable logistic regression and dose–response analysis to evaluate fall risk.  Nutrition (aOR = 5.10), mobility (aOR = 2.60), depression (aOR = 2.34), and vision (aOR = 2.21) impairments were independently associated with falls. Fall rates rose monotonically from 4.6% (one domain) to 29.1% (≥4 domains; p trend  An IC impairment count of ≥3, or specific clusters (nutrition, mobility, depression), provides practical triage criteria for community-based fall-prevention. These findings facilitate person-centred risk stratification and resource allocation within integrated care systems for super-aging societies.

archiveRecords.title: Real-world evidence on the management and outcomes of glioblastoma in elderly patients: a monocentric retrospective analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) carries a poor prognosis, and older patients and those with impaired performance status are often underrepresented in randomized trials. This study evaluated real-world treatment patterns, survival outcomes, and factors associated with outcome in older patients with GBM.  We retrospectively analyzed 63 patients aged ≥ 65 years with a diagnosis of GBM managed at a single-center radiation oncology department between 2014 and 2023. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were calculated from diagnosis. Multivariable Cox models included age, sex, Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), radiologically confirmed gross total resection (GTR), and temozolomide (TMZ) administration as clinically prespecified covariates. Complete-case analyses were performed. Proportional hazards assumptions were assessed using Schoenfeld residuals, with additional time-varying and exploratory sensitivity analyses addressing diagnostic classification, treatment selection, concomitant TMZ exposure, and treatment timing.  Median OS was 7.0 months (95% CI 5.3–14.4) and median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI 3.9–7.8). In the multivariable OS model ( n = 56; 50 deaths), increasing age was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.02–1.17; p = 0.011), whereas female sex was associated with a lower hazard of death (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.91; p = 0.025). Omission of TMZ was associated with higher mortality (HR 2.26, 95% CI 1.16–4.41; p = 0.017), while GTR showed a directionally favorable association that did not reach conventional statistical significance (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.27–1.01; p = 0.054). In the PFS model ( n = 56; 53 events), increasing age (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01–1.14; p = 0.027) and omission of TMZ (HR 2.34, 95% CI 1.20–4.55; p = 0.013) were associated with higher hazards, whereas female sex (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.89; p = 0.022) and higher KPS (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.96–1.00; p = 0.039) were associated with lower hazards. Resection status violated the proportional hazards assumption for PFS; time-varying analysis indicated an early favorable association of GTR that attenuated over time. Sensitivity analyses based on concomitant TMZ exposure and survival measured from radiotherapy initiation yielded similar associations.  Survival remained limited in this real-world cohort of older patients with GBM. Age, sex, performance status, resection status, and TMZ administration showed varying associations with outcome, with TMZ showing the most consistent association across analyses. Given the small retrospective cohort and substantial treatment selection, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

archiveRecords.title: Frailty and outcome after hospital admissions in two populations aged 80 years and above in 2012 and 2022 using the Hospital Frailty Risk Score
archiveRecords.abstract: Purpose To study outcomes in two cohorts of patients ≥ 80 years admitted to a tertiary hospital in Bergen Norway in 2012 and 2022.  This retrospective observational study compared two separate calendar-year cohorts of patients aged ≥ 80 years hospitalized in 2012 and 2022. Frailty was assessed using the ICD-10-based Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS). Outcomes included hospital length of stay, 30-day readmission, hospital mortality, and one-year survival after last admission. Survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier curves and Cox regression models.  There was an increase in patient admissions from 5112 (2012] to 6232 (2022] with a female majority. Half of both cohorts were classified as frail [HFRS > 15], with no significant sex difference. Non- frail patients had the highest one-year survival [87%] compared to 69% in the high frailty group. A higher mortality was found in frail males [65%] compared with females and in the age group ≥ 90 years. The combination of high frailty risk [HFRS > 15], age ≥ 90 years and male had the lowest survival of all sub-group analyzed [60%].  Higher HFRS was associated with worse clinical outcomes. The HFRS was able to identify vulnerable patient groups with significantly increased mortality, but there was no increase in frailty over the 10-year period in the two cohorts.

archiveRecords.title: Efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens in pulmonary tuberculosis patients aged 70 years and above: a retrospective study
archiveRecords.abstract: Older patients aged 70 years and above exhibit immunosenescence, increased comorbidity burden, and high susceptibility to adverse drug reactions. The standard HRZE regimen remains controversial in this population due to the considerable toxicity of pyrazinamide (PZA). This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone (FQ)-containing triple or quadruple regimens compared with conventional standard HR(L2)ZE or HR(L2)E regimens in older pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) patients, so as to provide evidence for individualized treatment strategies in older adults.  A total of 184 newly diagnosed PTB patients aged ≥ 70 years were enrolled in this single-center retrospective study in 2023. Patients were divided into four groups according to initial anti-tuberculosis regimens: standard HR(L2)ZE quadruple therapy group, HR(L2)E triple therapy group, FQ-containing quadruple group, and FQ-containing triple group. Treatment outcomes and adverse event rates were compared among groups. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify independent risk factors for treatment failure and adverse events. Propensity score matching (PSM) was further performed between the standard HR(L2)ZE and FQ-containing quadruple groups to minimize baseline selection bias.  Significant differences in treatment success rates and overall adverse event rates were observed among the four groups ( P P  For PTB patients aged 70 years and older, the conventional HR(L2)ZE standard regimen is associated with high toxicity and limited clinical applicability. FQ-containing triple and quadruple regimens were associated with more favorable treatment outcomes, while PZA omission was associated with a lower risk of adverse events. Individualized therapeutic strategies with prudent PZA use and rational selection of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens may be considered for older patients. Given the retrospective observational design and potential selection bias, the observed associations should not be interpreted as causal relationships and require confirmation in prospective multicenter studies. Trial registration Not applicable.

archiveRecords.title: Effects of multicomponent exercise combined with nutritional intervention on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: To systematically evaluate the effects of multicomponent exercise (ME) combined with nutritional intervention on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults.  A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published from inception to June 30, 2026. Participants were older adults aged ≥ 60 years. Interventions were required to include both ME and nutritional intervention. Primary outcomes were global cognitive function and depressive symptoms. Hedges‘ g was used as the effect size measure, and a random-effects model was prespecified as the primary model for all pooled analyses. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were also performed.  A total of 9 RCTs involving 1,814 participants were included. Of these, 7 studies contributed data on global cognitive function and 5 studies contributed data on depressive symptoms. Meta-analysis showed that ME combined with nutritional intervention may improve global cognitive function ( g = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.08 ~ 0.54) and depressive symptoms ( g = -0.51, 95% CI: -0.93~-0.09) in older adults, but moderate-to-high heterogeneity was observed in both global cognitive function ( I² = 68.54%) and depressive symptoms ( I² = 63.54%) analyses. Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant between-subgroup differences by nutrition type, baseline cognitive status, or exercise modality ( P > 0.05), and only intervention duration showed a significant subgroup difference for global cognitive function ( P  ME combined with nutritional intervention may have a small beneficial effect on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults. However, the current evidence is limited by the small number of included studies, moderate-to-high heterogeneity, underpowered subgroup analyses, and potential publication bias. The trim-and-fill-adjusted estimates for both global cognitive function and depressive symptoms were attenuated, and their 95% confidence intervals crossed zero, indicating sensitivity to potential publication bias. These  should be regarded as exploratory and interpreted with caution. Future high-quality RCTs with larger sample sizes, longer follow-up periods, and standardized intervention protocols are needed for validation.

archiveRecords.title: Toward Standardization of Intrinsic Capacity Assessment: A Methodological Comparison of the Responsiveness of Composite Scoring Methods
archiveRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used as an intervention outcome; however, IC composites lack a standardized scoring method, hindering comparisons across trials. To determine whether the scoring method influenced the detection of intervention effects, we applied multiple composite scoring approaches to the same data and compared their responsiveness to a 12-week exercise intervention in older adults at risk of mild cognitive impairment. : Pre- and post-intervention IC data were obtained from 59 community-dwelling older adults assigned to resistance training (n=34) or stretching and flexibility (n=25). The five-domain IC composite was computed repeatedly using alternative scoring approaches: z-score (concurrent and baseline-anchored variants), percentage of maximum possible (POMP), binary classification (0/1), and a three-category ordinal scale. Responsiveness was quantified using the standardized response mean (SRM). : Responsiveness ranged from negligible to large for identical data, indicating that the intervention effect depended on the scoring method. The ordinal and POMP composites were the most responsive (SRM 0.74–0.88 and 0.50–0.76). Within the z-score composite, responsiveness depended entirely on the standardization anchor: the concurrent specification was insensitive (SRM ≈ 0), whereas baseline-anchoring showed moderate responsiveness (0.62–0.71). The binary scoring was the least sensitive, showing a ceiling effect. : Ordinal three-category scoring was the most responsive, suggesting that approaches combining a fixed reference with a category-based structure are well suited for detecting change in IC. This finding requires confirmation against external criteria for IC, such as its predictive validity for adverse health outcomes, along with domain weighting and instrument selection.

archiveRecords.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
archiveRecords.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

archiveRecords.title: Intrinsic capacity among Hispanic older adults in the United States: Sociodemographic correlates and subgroup analyses
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used to conceptualize healthy aging. However, evidence on socio-demographic correlates in IC among Hispanic older adults in the United States remains limited. Research Design and  We analyzed data from a nationally sampled cohort from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, including Hispanic adults aged ≥60 years. IC was constructed from five domains. Multiple linear regression models examined associations between socio-demographic factors and IC, with stratified analyses by gender, community of residence, and place of birth.  The sample included 749 participants (60.08% female; 89.05% urban residents; 63.02% foreign-born), with a mean IC score of 6.49 (SD = 1.67). In the overall sample, being male, married/partnered, having a household income above $28,034, and being physically active were positively associated with IC, whereas having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC (all p  Physical activity and chronic disease burden were important correlates of IC among Hispanic older adults, with some subgroup-specific patterns observed across gender, residential community, and place of birth. These findings highlight the importance of considering demographic and contextual factors when promoting healthy aging among Hispanic older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Perceived Care Among Rural Left-Behind Older Adults in China: A Network Analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: Rural-to-urban migration separates many rural older adults from adult children and changes how care is received and experienced. Rural left-behind older adults remain in their rural places of origin after family members migrate for work.  This study examined conditional associations among reported care items and compared care networks by number of children and gender.  Cross-sectional data were obtained from 836 rural left-behind older adults aged 55 to 95 who completed the 14-item CSS-RLE. EBIC-LASSO Gaussian graphical models estimated item-level networks, expected influence summarized net signed connectivity, and network comparison tests assessed subgroup differences.  Village care and visits had the highest expected influence in the overall, male, and three-or-more-child networks. Holiday gifts from offspring ranked highest in the one- and two-child networks, whereas living expenses from children ranked highest in the female network. Network structure differed between one-child and larger-family groups and between men and women.

archiveRecords.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary : (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content.  revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. However, older adults recalled as many episodic details as younger participants. There was no difference as a function of the recipient's age. Overall, these  underscore the value of studying memory in everyday social contexts.
