archiveRecords.title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.  Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.  EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.  We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.

archiveRecords.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

archiveRecords.title: Deprescribing Fall Risk–Increasing Drugs in Older Adults: Implementation Challenges and a Conceptual Framework from the DeFRID Trial and Global Evidence
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Deprescribing fall risk–increasing drugs (FRIDs) is essential for reducing polypharmacy and falls in older adults, yet randomized controlled trials (RCTs) face unique implementation challenges. The DeFRID study is an ongoing multi-center RCT evaluating an ARMOR-based deprescribing intervention versus usual care in adults aged ≥60 years prescribed FRIDs. The  of this review are threefold: (1) to describe practical challenges encountered during a multi-center deprescribing RCT in India; (2) to propose a conceptual framework for categorizing these barriers; and (3) to contextualize DeFRID's experience within the broader deprescribing research landscape.  We conducted a narrative review with systematic scoping elements, synthesizing global RCT evidence from PubMed, OpenAlex, and Google Scholar (inception–December 2025) with DeFRID process evaluation data. DeFRID barriers and facilitators were identified via mixed- (clinician KAP questionnaire and qualitative interviews), team meetings, retention logs, and Phase II RCT implementation data, thematically categorized, then compared with global RCT challenges.  DeFRID implementation revealed four challenge categories: ethical–clinical difficulties establishing equipoise for FRID withdrawal; operational barriers to recruitment and retention; methodological complexities in fall outcome ascertainment; and context-specific constraints unique to the Indian LMIC setting—limited deprescribing guidelines, polypharmacy normalization, fragmented care coordination, and hierarchical decision-making. Global RCTs revealed substantial implementation challenges: low clinician adherence, short follow-up periods, restrictive eligibility excluding frail or cognitively impaired older adults, and resource-intensive interventions limiting scalability.  Deprescribing FRIDs in older adults is impeded by ethical, operational, methodological, and provider-patient challenges, necessitating multilevel strategies integrating training, shared decision-making, context-specific guidelines, and stakeholder engagement for scalable implementation.

archiveRecords.title: Vulnerability Intersections: An Integrative Conceptual Framework for Understanding Vulnerability in AI-Assisted Care for Older Adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.

archiveRecords.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

archiveRecords.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
archiveRecords.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

archiveRecords.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.

archiveRecords.title: Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Low vitamin D and B12 levels are linked to low self-reported sleep quality and conditions comorbid with sleep disturbances in older adults. We examined the associations between serum vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep indices in middle-aged and older adults.  We studied 460 participants aged 40 and older (70.9 ± 12.0 [SD] years; 52.8% female; 22.2% Black) in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Predictors included total serum vitamin D and B12, sleep outcomes included total sleep time (TST, minutes), sleep efficiency (SE, %), sleep onset latency (minutes), wake after sleep onset (WASO, minutes), and average wake bout length (WBL, minutes). We examined race and sex as effect modifiers of associations between vitamins and sleep.  Higher vitamin D concentration was associated with longer TST (B = 23.63 minutes, 95% CI, 9.62-37.64) and shorter WBL (B = −0.29 minutes, 95% CI, −0.50 to −0.09). Vitamin D deficiency was associated with shorter TST (B= −23.03 minutes, 95% CI, −42.05 to −4.01). The associations between vitamin D and sleep were stronger among Black participants. Higher B12 was associated with shorter WASO in women but longer WASO in men. B12 insufficiency/deficiency was associated with longer TST in men but shorter TST in women.  Higher vitamin D levels are associated with longer and less disturbed sleep in middle-aged and older adults. Future studies are needed to understand if maintaining optimal vitamin D levels improve sleep quality and promote better sleep-associated health outcomes.

archiveRecords.title: Planetary Health Diet Adherence and Frailty in Older Adults: Evidence from the Seniors-ENRICA Cohorts
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Frailty is a major determinant of disability and adverse outcomes in older adults. The Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a plant-based dietary pattern promoting environmental sustainability, has been associated with lower mortality and reduced chronic disease risk. We examined the association between adherence to the Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) and frailty over time using repeated frailty assessments.  Data came from two cohorts of community-dwelling older adults: Seniors-ENRICA-1 (2008-2015; ≥60 years; n = 3,289) and Seniors-ENRICA-2 (2015-2023; ≥65 years; n = 3,273). Baseline diet was assessed using a validated diet history, and adherence to the PHD was assessed using the PHDI (0-140), based on 15 food groups. Frailty was defined by the Fried phenotype (≥3 criteria of exhaustion, low physical activity, slow gait, muscle weakness, unintentional weight loss). Generalized estimating equation (GEE) models estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for frailty across PHDI tertiles, adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors.  Higher PHDI adherence was consistently associated with lower odds of frailty over time. Comparing highest vs. lowest tertiles, multivariable-adjusted ORs (95% CI) were 0.62 (0.42, 0.92) in Seniors-ENRICA-1, 0.40 (0.24, 0.65) in Seniors-ENRICA-2 and 0.52 (0.38, 0.70) in the pooled analyses. Higher PHDI adherence was primarily associated with lower odds of low physical activity, while vegetables and fruits showed the strongest independent associations among individual PHDI components.  Greater PHDI adherence is associated with lower odds of frailty in Spanish older adults, supporting the potential role of sustainable, plant-based dietary patterns for healthy ageing.

reviewRecords.title: Diagnostic performance of calculated serum osmolarity versus clinical impression for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients
reviewRecords.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and agreement of calculated serum osmolarity for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients, using clinical impression of dehydration as the reference standard, and to examine glucose levels across concordant and discordant classification groups. Design and setting This prospective, observational study was conducted in a geriatric acute care unit. Participants The study included 455 older hospitalized patients with a mean age of 82.2 ± 6.8 years and 70% were female. Measurements Clinical impression of dehydration (dehydration vs. no dehydration [normal hydration + hyperhydration]) was judged and recorded by the attending physician within 24 h of admission. Calculated serum osmolarity was derived from routine laboratory values and classified as high (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) or normal (  Clinically, 23% of patients were classified as dehydrated. High calculated osmolarity occurred in 38%. Using the ≥ 295 mOsmol/l cut-off, sensitivity was 48.6% and specificity 65.1%; positive and negative predictive values were 29.7% and 80.7%, respectively, and accuracy was 61.3%. Agreement beyond chance was poor (κ = 0.112). Mean glucose was higher in osmolarity-positive groups, including false positives (all p  In older hospitalized patients, calculated serum osmolarity (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) showed limited agreement with clinical dehydration assessment with frequent osmolarity-positive classifications in clinically non-dehydrated patients. These findings support cautious clinical interpretation of calculated osmolarity in acute care, particularly when glucose is elevated.

reviewRecords.title: Body weight following a multidomain lifestyle intervention in older adults at risk of dementia – A post-hoc analysis of the AgeWell.de-trial
reviewRecords.abstract: Lifestyle interventions provide a promising approach to address higher body weight as a risk factor for dementia.  The AgeWell.de-trial was primarily designed to preserve cognitive function and reduce dementia risk. In this post-hoc analysis, we investigated body weight following the multidomain intervention among older adults with overweight or obesity, as well as the role of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss.  Analyses used data from the cluster-randomized AgeWell.de-trial, testing a multidomain intervention (dietary counselling, enhancement of physical, social and cognitive activity, medication review, intervention for cardiovascular risk factors, depressive symptoms/grief, if applicable) over 24 months in adults aged 60 to 77 years at risk for dementia. Associations between intervention allocation and body weight at follow-up were analyzed using linear regression, controlling for covariates, based on multiply imputed data.  The sample included n = 678 participants with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², mean age (SD): 68.9 (4.8), 52.1% female. Group allocation was not associated with body weight at 24-month follow-up (b (unstandardized regression coefficient) = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.51; 1.11). Older age (b = -0.14, 95% CI: -0.25; -0.03) and a high level of education (b = -1.28, 95% CI: -2.55; 0.00) were linked to lower body weight at follow-up, while higher baseline body weight predicted higher body weight at follow-up (b = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.91; 0.98). Levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss remained high but stable in both groups, regardless of group allocation.  In this post-hoc analysis, group allocation was not associated with lower body weight at follow-up. Despite high levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss and favorable changes in diet and physical activity in the intervention group, these changes did not translate into measurable weight loss. Trial registration AgeWell.de was prospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register on December 7th, 2017 (DRKS trial identifier DRKS00013555).

reviewRecords.title: Enhanced person profiles: a cluster randomised trial protocol for Swiss long-term care facilities
reviewRecords.abstract: Family participation and teamwork are crucial components of person-centred dementia care in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) and are therefore widely recommended. However, these often remain ad hoc and staff-dependent in LTCF settings. Robust evidence on reproducible whole-team models for family participation and their impact on the quality of life of people with dementia is limited. The person profile is a complex intervention that has been tested under randomised controlled trial conditions, but family participation and teamwork were identified as weak areas in this intervention. Consequently, we developed the enhanced person profile. This programme incorporates clinical tools for routine family participation and psychological safety  that enhance teamwork, ultimately aiming to improve the quality of life of people with dementia.  We will conduct a two-period, two-sequence cluster randomised crossover trial in 20 LTCFs in German-speaking Switzerland with 260 people with dementia. Each period will last 7 months, separated by a 1-month washout. Clusters will follow one of two sequences (intervention → usual care or usual care → intervention). The primary outcome will be proxy-rated quality of life (QUALIDEM). Secondary outcomes will comprise symptoms and concerns (Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale for People with Dementia (IPOS-Dem)), person-centred care (Person-Centred Practice Inventory – Staff Short Form (PCPI-S SF)), perceived family participation (FICS-T), and teamwork (Team Climate Inventory (TCI); unit). Our analyses will be carried out using linear mixed-effects models under the intention-to-treat principle, accounting for clustering and repeated measures. A mixed- process evaluation will be employed to examine implementation, mechanisms, and context, with qualitative follow-up exploring sustainability. Discussion This trial, embedded in routine LTCF care, will assess the effects of the enhanced person profile on the quality of life of people with dementia and determine its mechanisms of action as well as implementation requirements for large-scale adoption. Trial registration This trial was registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00041653). The Berne Cantonal Ethics Committee (lead committee) reviewed and approved the protocol and study documents, including the consent forms, educational materials, and electronic case report forms (BASEC-ID: 2026 − 00761).

reviewRecords.title: Real-world evidence on the management and outcomes of glioblastoma in elderly patients: a monocentric retrospective analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) carries a poor prognosis, and older patients and those with impaired performance status are often underrepresented in randomized trials. This study evaluated real-world treatment patterns, survival outcomes, and factors associated with outcome in older patients with GBM.  We retrospectively analyzed 63 patients aged ≥ 65 years with a diagnosis of GBM managed at a single-center radiation oncology department between 2014 and 2023. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were calculated from diagnosis. Multivariable Cox models included age, sex, Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), radiologically confirmed gross total resection (GTR), and temozolomide (TMZ) administration as clinically prespecified covariates. Complete-case analyses were performed. Proportional hazards assumptions were assessed using Schoenfeld residuals, with additional time-varying and exploratory sensitivity analyses addressing diagnostic classification, treatment selection, concomitant TMZ exposure, and treatment timing.  Median OS was 7.0 months (95% CI 5.3–14.4) and median PFS was 5.3 months (95% CI 3.9–7.8). In the multivariable OS model ( n = 56; 50 deaths), increasing age was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.02–1.17; p = 0.011), whereas female sex was associated with a lower hazard of death (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.91; p = 0.025). Omission of TMZ was associated with higher mortality (HR 2.26, 95% CI 1.16–4.41; p = 0.017), while GTR showed a directionally favorable association that did not reach conventional statistical significance (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.27–1.01; p = 0.054). In the PFS model ( n = 56; 53 events), increasing age (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01–1.14; p = 0.027) and omission of TMZ (HR 2.34, 95% CI 1.20–4.55; p = 0.013) were associated with higher hazards, whereas female sex (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.89; p = 0.022) and higher KPS (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.96–1.00; p = 0.039) were associated with lower hazards. Resection status violated the proportional hazards assumption for PFS; time-varying analysis indicated an early favorable association of GTR that attenuated over time. Sensitivity analyses based on concomitant TMZ exposure and survival measured from radiotherapy initiation yielded similar associations.  Survival remained limited in this real-world cohort of older patients with GBM. Age, sex, performance status, resection status, and TMZ administration showed varying associations with outcome, with TMZ showing the most consistent association across analyses. Given the small retrospective cohort and substantial treatment selection, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

reviewRecords.title: Efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens in pulmonary tuberculosis patients aged 70 years and above: a retrospective study
reviewRecords.abstract: Older patients aged 70 years and above exhibit immunosenescence, increased comorbidity burden, and high susceptibility to adverse drug reactions. The standard HRZE regimen remains controversial in this population due to the considerable toxicity of pyrazinamide (PZA). This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone (FQ)-containing triple or quadruple regimens compared with conventional standard HR(L2)ZE or HR(L2)E regimens in older pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) patients, so as to provide evidence for individualized treatment strategies in older adults.  A total of 184 newly diagnosed PTB patients aged ≥ 70 years were enrolled in this single-center retrospective study in 2023. Patients were divided into four groups according to initial anti-tuberculosis regimens: standard HR(L2)ZE quadruple therapy group, HR(L2)E triple therapy group, FQ-containing quadruple group, and FQ-containing triple group. Treatment outcomes and adverse event rates were compared among groups. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify independent risk factors for treatment failure and adverse events. Propensity score matching (PSM) was further performed between the standard HR(L2)ZE and FQ-containing quadruple groups to minimize baseline selection bias.  Significant differences in treatment success rates and overall adverse event rates were observed among the four groups ( P P  For PTB patients aged 70 years and older, the conventional HR(L2)ZE standard regimen is associated with high toxicity and limited clinical applicability. FQ-containing triple and quadruple regimens were associated with more favorable treatment outcomes, while PZA omission was associated with a lower risk of adverse events. Individualized therapeutic strategies with prudent PZA use and rational selection of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens may be considered for older patients. Given the retrospective observational design and potential selection bias, the observed associations should not be interpreted as causal relationships and require confirmation in prospective multicenter studies. reviewRecords.title: Effects of multicomponent exercise combined with nutritional intervention on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: To systematically evaluate the effects of multicomponent exercise (ME) combined with nutritional intervention on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults.  A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published from inception to June 30, 2026. Participants were older adults aged ≥ 60 years. Interventions were required to include both ME and nutritional intervention. Primary outcomes were global cognitive function and depressive symptoms. Hedges‘ g was used as the effect size measure, and a random-effects model was prespecified as the primary model for all pooled analyses. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses were also performed.  A total of 9 RCTs involving 1,814 participants were included. Of these, 7 studies contributed data on global cognitive function and 5 studies contributed data on depressive symptoms. Meta-analysis showed that ME combined with nutritional intervention may improve global cognitive function ( g = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.08 ~ 0.54) and depressive symptoms ( g = -0.51, 95% CI: -0.93~-0.09) in older adults, but moderate-to-high heterogeneity was observed in both global cognitive function ( I² = 68.54%) and depressive symptoms ( I² = 63.54%) analyses. Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant between-subgroup differences by nutrition type, baseline cognitive status, or exercise modality ( P > 0.05), and only intervention duration showed a significant subgroup difference for global cognitive function ( P  ME combined with nutritional intervention may have a small beneficial effect on global cognitive function and depressive symptoms in older adults. However, the current evidence is limited by the small number of included studies, moderate-to-high heterogeneity, underpowered subgroup analyses, and potential publication bias. The trim-and-fill-adjusted estimates for both global cognitive function and depressive symptoms were attenuated, and their 95% confidence intervals crossed zero, indicating sensitivity to potential publication bias. These  should be regarded as exploratory and interpreted with caution. Future high-quality RCTs with larger sample sizes, longer follow-up periods, and standardized intervention protocols are needed for validation.

reviewRecords.title: Toward Standardization of Intrinsic Capacity Assessment: A Methodological Comparison of the Responsiveness of Composite Scoring Methods
reviewRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used as an intervention outcome; however, IC composites lack a standardized scoring method, hindering comparisons across trials. To determine whether the scoring method influenced the detection of intervention effects, we applied multiple composite scoring approaches to the same data and compared their responsiveness to a 12-week exercise intervention in older adults at risk of mild cognitive impairment. : Pre- and post-intervention IC data were obtained from 59 community-dwelling older adults assigned to resistance training (n=34) or stretching and flexibility (n=25). The five-domain IC composite was computed repeatedly using alternative scoring approaches: z-score (concurrent and baseline-anchored variants), percentage of maximum possible (POMP), binary classification (0/1), and a three-category ordinal scale. Responsiveness was quantified using the standardized response mean (SRM). : Responsiveness ranged from negligible to large for identical data, indicating that the intervention effect depended on the scoring method. The ordinal and POMP composites were the most responsive (SRM 0.74–0.88 and 0.50–0.76). Within the z-score composite, responsiveness depended entirely on the standardization anchor: the concurrent specification was insensitive (SRM ≈ 0), whereas baseline-anchoring showed moderate responsiveness (0.62–0.71). The binary scoring was the least sensitive, showing a ceiling effect. : Ordinal three-category scoring was the most responsive, suggesting that approaches combining a fixed reference with a category-based structure are well suited for detecting change in IC. This finding requires confirmation against external criteria for IC, such as its predictive validity for adverse health outcomes, along with domain weighting and instrument selection.

reviewRecords.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
reviewRecords.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

reviewRecords.title: Perceived Care Among Rural Left-Behind Older Adults in China: A Network Analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: Rural-to-urban migration separates many rural older adults from adult children and changes how care is received and experienced. Rural left-behind older adults remain in their rural places of origin after family members migrate for work.  This study examined conditional associations among reported care items and compared care networks by number of children and gender.  Cross-sectional data were obtained from 836 rural left-behind older adults aged 55 to 95 who completed the 14-item CSS-RLE. EBIC-LASSO Gaussian graphical models estimated item-level networks, expected influence summarized net signed connectivity, and network comparison tests assessed subgroup differences.  Village care and visits had the highest expected influence in the overall, male, and three-or-more-child networks. Holiday gifts from offspring ranked highest in the one- and two-child networks, whereas living expenses from children ranked highest in the female network. Network structure differed between one-child and larger-family groups and between men and women.

reviewRecords.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

reviewRecords.title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary : (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content.  revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. However, older adults recalled as many episodic details as younger participants. There was no difference as a function of the recipient's age. Overall, these  underscore the value of studying memory in everyday social contexts.

reviewRecords.title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.  Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.  EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.  We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.

reviewRecords.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

reviewRecords.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

reviewRecords.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
reviewRecords.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

reviewRecords.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.
